lines.text: Chapter one, section eight. Test yourself.
Here are three quick questions to see whether the leverage lens has clicked for you.
Question one. You are in position on the turn holding a hand that will be a value bet on roughly one third of rivers and a bluff on the rest. Should you bet the turn?

Think it through: your hand is currently polarized in a way that mirrors a bluff, but future value gives you leverage. Betting is right, because the threat of a value bet on future rivers gives your turn bluffs additional expected value.

Question two. You are out of position facing a turn bet. The board is very dynamic, and many rivers will change the value of both players' hands. Should you call more or fewer of your medium-strength hands than you would on a static board?
Fewer. On a dynamic board, the leverage from the incoming river bet is heavier, because your hand's value can crumble on rivers that give your opponent's polarized range more equity.

Question three. You are the aggressor with an eight-dollar stack and a two-dollar pot, planning to bet the turn and the river with a polarized range. What is roughly the correct turn bet size to plan for a geometric river shove?
Two dollars, or full pot, because that turns the river pot into six dollars and lets you shove your remaining six-dollar stack cleanly.
If you got most of those right, you are already thinking about the turn the way this book wants you to.
If not, do not worry: the ideas will get many more concrete reps in the chapters to come.
